title: ZPD-SCA: Unveiling the Blind Spots of LLMs in Assessing Students’ Cognitive Abilities
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can accurately assess the developmental appropriateness of Chinese reading materials for students at different school stages, framed through Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD). The core question is whether LLMs can judge how well a text aligns with students’ cognitive abilities across elementary, middle, and high school levels, rather than whether the models improve student reading outcomes. The authors argue that educational applications often assume LLMs understand student cognitive differences, but that assumption has not been rigorously tested, especially for Chinese reading comprehension.

To study this, the authors introduce a benchmark called ZPD-SCA, a dataset for three-way classification of Chinese texts into elementary, middle, or high school appropriateness. The corpus was assembled from real-world extracurricular reading materials spanning 12 genres and over 8 million characters before filtering to a final 4.7 million-character labeled set. Annotation was carried out by 60 nationally recognized “Special Grade” teachers in China, with each book evaluated by at least 20 annotators. The paper evaluates 10 LLMs under zero-shot prompting, in-context learning, and for one model, LoRA fine-tuning, using metrics such as accuracy, F1, cross-level migration concentration, and weighted directional bias.

The population and context are K-12 educational stages in China, specifically Chinese-language reading materials intended for elementary, middle, and high school students. The study does not involve a classroom intervention or direct student outcome measurement; instead, it uses expert-annotated benchmark data to test model performance on educational judgment tasks. Teachers contribute as expert annotators, and students are represented indirectly through school-stage labels rather than as active participants receiving an instructional treatment.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs are limited in their ability to align reading materials with students’ cognitive levels in zero-shot settings, with some models performing at or below random-guessing levels. Performance improves substantially with in-context examples and targeted fine-tuning, suggesting that the limitation is not total incapacity but insufficient task-specific training. Even so, the best-performing models still show systematic directional biases and uneven performance across genres, indicating that LLMs are not yet reliable for cognitively aligned educational judgments without additional adaptation. For the targeted evidence question on generative AI and foundational reading outcomes, this is a near-miss study: it concerns reading-material difficulty assessment, not causal evidence on student foundational reading outcomes such as phonics, decoding, fluency, vocabulary, or comprehension gains.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical benchmark/model evaluation study with clear methods, but it does not test a causal educational intervention on K-12 students and reports no randomized or quasi-experimental learner outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows unclear practical educational impact: it demonstrates benchmark performance gains for LLM text-level assessment with prompting/fine-tuning, but provides no direct evidence of impact on student literacy outcomes or classroom effectiveness.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking large language models on classifying Chinese reading texts by developmental appropriateness (elementary, middle, high school) to assess alignment with students' cognitive abilities rather than delivering instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluates LLM accuracy in judging stage-appropriate Chinese reading comprehension difficulty, not student reading improvement. In zero-shot settings, some models performed very poorly, with GLM and Qwen-max below random-guess accuracy for a 3-class task (<33% ACC), while performance improved substantially with in-context learning; for example, Qwen-max rose from 0.3061 to 0.6296 ACC and GLM from 0.2659 to 0.6878 ACC on the benchmark. The benchmark was annotated by 60 elite teachers and reduced to a 4.7 million-character labeled corpus, but no K-12 learner outcome data or causal literacy effects are reported.
finding.measure: Model performance on benchmarked reading-difficulty/stage classification (accuracy, F1, CLME, WDBI) for Chinese texts
